title: How a system design interview works and is scored
scopeHtml:
Scope: what the round tests, scoring axes, timeline, round types, interviewer signals, preparation plan.

notes.title: What a system design interview really tests
notes.html:
The interview is not a quiz about one right answer. It is a 45 to 60 minute conversation that shows how you think when the problem is vague. The interviewer wants to see whether you can take "design Instagram" and turn it into requirements, numbers, a sensible architecture and honest trade-offs, while staying calm and collaborative.

There is no single correct design. Two candidates can draw different boxes and both pass, if each one can defend the choices with numbers and say what breaks.

Worked example. Prompt: "Design a URL shortener." A weak start is drawing a database at once. A strong start asks: how many new URLs per day (say 100M), read to write ratio (say 100:1), how long links live (5 years), custom aliases needed? Those four answers give 100M / 86,400 = about 1,160 writes/s, about 116,000 reads/s, and 100M x 365 x 5 = 182B rows. That already says "this is a read-heavy key-value problem that needs caching and sharding".

Industry examples. Big-tech loops (Google, Meta, Amazon, Uber, Stripe, Swiggy) all have a design round for senior engineers. The rubric differs in wording but the shape is the same: scoping, structure, depth, trade-offs, communication.

Everyday analogy. It is like an architect meeting a client: you do not start laying bricks, you ask how many people will live there and what the budget is.

Common interview traps.

  • Treating it like an exam and hunting for "the answer" instead of driving a conversation.
  • Starting to draw before asking a single question.
  • Memorising the design of one famous system and forcing every prompt into it.

notes.title: How you are scored
notes.html:
Most companies score you on a handful of axes, each rated separately, and then combine them. Typical axes:

Axis What a strong signal looks like
Problem scoping Clarifies functional and non-functional requirements, states assumptions
Estimation Quick, sensible numbers that steer the design
Architecture Clean components, correct data flow, right storage choices
Depth Goes deep on 1 or 2 hard parts (not shallow on everything)
Trade-offs Names alternatives, says why chosen, what breaks
Communication Structured, checks in, takes hints, writes legibly
Operations Monitoring, failure handling, rollout, cost

Level matters. For a 3-year developer moving to senior, the bar is: you own the design end to end, you see the next bottleneck before it appears, and you choose boring technology unless there is a reason. A staff candidate is also expected to talk about org cost, migrations and multi-year evolution.

Decision gravity. The decision here is where you spend your time. Spending 20 of 45 minutes on the API and schema leaves no room for depth, which is the axis that separates senior from mid. This is reversible within the interview: you can say "let me move on, we can return to this".

Everyday analogy. A figure skating score: technical points for the correct design, presentation points for how you explain it.

Common interview traps.

  • Optimising only for a "correct" architecture and forgetting that communication is scored on its own.
  • Going wide and shallow: ten boxes, no deep dive.
  • Ignoring the level: a senior answer without failure modes reads as mid-level.

notes.title: The usual timeline of 45 minutes
notes.html:
A rough budget keeps you from running out of time on the interesting part.

 0-5   min  Requirements and scope (functional, non-functional)
 5-10  min  Estimation and API / data model
10-20  min  High-level design (boxes and arrows, one main flow)
20-38  min  Deep dives (2 areas the interviewer cares about)
38-43  min  Bottlenecks, failures, trade-offs, monitoring
43-45  min  Summary, questions

Worked example. Design a chat app in 45 minutes: 4 min asking (1:1 and group, delivery receipts, 50M DAU), 5 min numbers (50M x 40 messages = 2B messages/day = about 23,000/s avg, 70,000/s peak), 8 min boxes (gateway, chat service, message store, push), then 18 min on the hard parts (ordering, offline delivery, WebSocket fan-out), then 10 min on failures and scale. The deep dive is the largest block.

Industry examples. Interview platforms and prep guides at companies such as Meta and Google describe a similar split, often with the interviewer steering the middle section. Treat the minutes as a guide, not a rule: if the interviewer jumps into a deep dive early, follow.

Everyday analogy. Planning a road trip: pick destination (scope), check distance and fuel (numbers), choose route (design), then handle the tricky mountain pass (deep dive).

Common interview traps.

  • Spending 15 minutes on estimates and never drawing a component.
  • Refusing to follow the interviewer's pivot because "I have not finished my plan".
  • No wrap-up; the last thing the interviewer hears is a half-finished detail.

notes.title: Types of rounds you will meet
notes.html:
"System design" is a family of rounds. Knowing which one you are in changes the plan.

  • HLD (high-level design): boxes, data flow, storage, scale. The classic "design Twitter".
  • LLD / machine coding: classes, interfaces, patterns, runnable code. "Design a parking lot."
  • API design: endpoints, pagination, idempotency, versioning.
  • Deep-dive on your own project: "Walk me through the architecture of what you built". Expect "why not X?" at every box.
  • Domain-specific: for you, Android: offline sync, image loading, push, large lists, analytics SDK design.

Worked example. A mobile-flavoured prompt: "Design the Android client of a photo feed." Scope: infinite scroll, offline cache, upload with retry. Numbers: 20 posts per page, thumbnails 30 KB each, so one page is 600 KB on 4G (about 0.1 s of transfer at 50 Mbps plus latency). Design: Paging 3 with a Room cache as single source of truth, WorkManager for uploads. The backend is a smaller part of that round.

Industry examples. Uber and Swiggy often use domain prompts (dispatch, delivery tracking). Stripe leans toward API design and idempotency. Google tends to emphasise scale and data structures.

Everyday analogy. A driving test has a written part and a road part; both are "driving" but need different prep.

Common interview traps.

  • Answering a mobile design with only backend boxes.
  • Assuming HLD depth in an LLD round (they want classes and code).

notes.title: Signals interviewers write down
notes.html:
Interviewers take notes in small concrete phrases. Knowing them lets you produce them on purpose.

Positive signals:

  • "Asked about read/write ratio before choosing storage."
  • "Gave numbers and used them to decide on a cache."
  • "Named the failure mode of the queue unprompted."
  • "Took a hint and adjusted gracefully."

Negative signals:

  • "Chose Kafka without saying why."
  • "Could not explain how consistency is kept between cache and DB."
  • "Dismissed the interviewer's concern instead of engaging."
  • "Silent for long periods."

Decision gravity. Naming a technology is cheap; defending it is what scores. Each technology pick is a reversible interview decision but represents a potentially one-way door in real life (a database choice is hard to undo). Say that out loud: "choosing Postgres first, can move to sharding later, but changing the primary key scheme later is painful".

Worked example. "I would use Redis for the feed cache: 100M users x 800 posts of 8-byte IDs = 640 GB, too big for one node, so I cluster it (for example 16 nodes of 64 GB) and cache only the active 20% of users, about 130 GB."

Industry examples. Twitter's timeline cache stores lists of tweet IDs per user in Redis, not whole tweets; mentioning that kind of detail is the "senior signal".

Everyday analogy. A teacher gives marks for showing the working, not only the final answer.

Common interview traps.

  • Buzzword lists (Kafka, Redis, Cassandra) with no why.
  • Thinking aloud so little that the interviewer cannot give credit.

notes.title: How to prepare in practice
notes.html:
Preparation is mostly pattern recognition plus drilling the framework. Learn the building blocks (load balancer, cache, queue, shard, replica, CDN), then practise assembling them against 15 to 20 classic prompts.

A workable plan over four weeks:

  1. Week 1: building blocks and numbers (this track and H1).
  2. Week 2: storage, caching, messaging deep dives.
  3. Week 3: ten classic problems, written on paper in 45 minutes each.
  4. Week 4: mock interviews with a friend; record yourself once.

Worked example. Ten problems at 45 minutes plus 15 minutes of review is 10 hours, which fits in two weekends. The review step (compare your design to a reference and list what you missed) is where most learning happens.

Industry examples. Public engineering blogs are the best free reference: Uber's and Netflix's tech blogs, Meta's engineering posts, the Kafka and Cassandra papers. Read how real systems made trade-offs rather than only watching walk-throughs.

Everyday analogy. Learning chess: you study openings (blocks), then play games (mocks), then review your mistakes.

Common interview traps.

  • Only watching videos and never drawing on a blank page yourself.
  • Memorising designs instead of reasons.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• The round tests structured thinking under ambiguity, not a single right design.
  • Scored on scoping, estimation, architecture, depth, trade-offs, communication and operations.
  • Budget about 45 minutes: scope, numbers, boxes, deep dives, wrap up. Follow the interviewer's pivots.
  • Know the round type: HLD, LLD, API, project deep dive, mobile.
  • Every technology pick needs a reason, an alternative and a failure mode.
  • Prepare with blocks, numbers, ten or more timed problems and mocks.

questions.promptHtml: What is a system design interview actually testing? Is there a "correct" architecture I am expected to arrive at?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Candidates who think it is a quiz hunt for the memorised answer and stop collaborating. I want to see if you understand the format.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: There is no single correct design. It is a 45 to 60 minute conversation that tests whether I can take a vague prompt, turn it into requirements and numbers, propose a sensible architecture, and defend it with honest trade-offs. Two candidates can draw different boxes and both pass if each can say why and what breaks.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The prompt is vague on purpose ("design Instagram"). The real task is to reduce ambiguity, in this order:

Vague prompt -> Requirements -> Numbers -> Design -> Deep dives -> Trade-offs

Example: "Design a URL shortener". Four questions (100M new URLs/day, 100:1 read:write, 5 year retention, custom aliases?) give about 1,160 writes/s, about 116,000 reads/s and 182B rows. That already says "read-heavy key-value store with a cache, sharded". The numbers did the design thinking.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Hunting for "the answer" instead of driving a conversation.
  • Drawing a database before asking a single question.
  • Forcing every prompt into the one famous design you memorised.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if my design differs from the interviewer's reference? -> Fine if I can defend it with numbers and name the failure mode.
  2. What is the first thing you do after hearing the prompt? -> Ask the 3 to 5 questions that change the design (scale, read/write ratio, consistency, scope).
  3. How does a wrong-but-reasoned design score against a textbook design with no reasoning? -> Usually better; the reasoning is what is scored.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer lists components that "should be there". The senior answer says the round tests how I structure ambiguity, and shows it by scoping first, using numbers to decide, and naming trade-offs unprompted.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: The same skill is a design doc: goals and non-goals, scale, alternatives, risks. Teams that skip scoping build the wrong thing at the wrong scale.

questions.promptHtml: How are you typically scored in a system design round, and how does the bar change from mid-level to senior?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether the candidate knows the rubric and so allocates effort across axes rather than only on the architecture.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Usually separate ratings on problem scoping, estimation, architecture, depth, trade-offs, communication and operations, then combined into a hire decision. At senior level the bar is that I own the design end to end, see the next bottleneck before it appears, and prefer boring technology unless I have a reason.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Axis            Strong signal
Scoping         clarifies functional + non-functional, states assumptions
Estimation      quick numbers that steer the design
Architecture    clean components, right data flow, right storage
Depth           deep on 1-2 hard parts, not shallow on ten
Trade-offs      alternatives, why chosen, what breaks
Communication   structured, checks in, takes hints
Operations      monitoring, failure handling, rollout, cost

Each axis is rated on its own, so a brilliant design with silent, disorganised delivery still loses points. Depth is the axis that most separates senior from mid. Staff level adds org cost, migrations and multi-year evolution.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Optimising only for architecture; communication is scored separately.
  • Going wide and shallow: ten boxes, no deep dive.
  • A senior answer with no failure modes reads as mid-level.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do you spend your time? -> Most of it in 1 to 2 deep dives, because depth is the differentiator.
  2. Is "I would spend 20 of 45 minutes on schema" a reversible choice? -> Within the interview yes ("let me move on and return"), but it costs the depth axis.
  3. What extra is expected at staff level? -> Org cost, migration plan, evolution over years, who owns what.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Mid: "the correct architecture". Senior: "seven axes, each scored; I deliberately produce a signal on each: assumptions, numbers, one deep dive, a failure story, and a cost remark".

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Design reviews at work use the same axes informally; reviews fail most often on missing operations and trade-offs, not on missing boxes.

questions.contextHtml: You are 22 minutes into a 45-minute "design a chat app" round (50M DAU, 1:1 and group, delivery receipts). You have spent that time writing a full SQL schema with indexes and a REST API with 12 endpoints. No boxes are drawn yet. The interviewer glances at the clock and says nothing.
questions.promptHtml: What do you do right now, and what should the time have looked like?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Keep going, the schema is important." This leaves 23 minutes for architecture, deep dives and wrap-up, so depth (the senior-separating axis) never happens.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: None needed; I ask the interviewer "I have gone deep on the data model; may I switch to the high-level flow and come back to the schema if useful?" to share the timing out loud.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop, summarise the 3 entities and 3 endpoints that matter, and move to a 5-minute high-level picture: gateway, chat service, message store, push.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Why I overran: I started with schema before scope; I treated API as exhaustive; I was not watching the clock.
  4. How I'd verify each: Put the budget on the whiteboard: scope 0-5, numbers and API 5-10, high-level 10-20, deep dives 20-38, wrap-up 38-45.
  5. Root cause: No explicit budget and starting with the part I was comfortable with.
  6. Fix: Chat example numbers in 2 minutes: 50M x 40 messages = 2B/day, about 23,000/s average, about 70,000/s peak. Then deep dive on ordering, offline delivery and WebSocket fan-out for the remaining time.
  7. Prevention: Practise with a visible timer; show only 3 to 5 endpoints.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not apologise at length or restart; I would not abandon the schema entirely, since access patterns matter for the message store.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The interviewer says "I actually like the schema, keep going" -> Follow the interviewer; the minutes are a guide, then I still protect 5 minutes for wrap-up.
  • You realise at minute 40 you skipped failure modes -> Spend the last 4 minutes on SPOFs, queue lag, monitoring, rather than saying "it is fine".

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a strong engineer spent 25 minutes on message ID generation and got "no signal on architecture or operations". The feedback was not that the depth was wrong, but that the budget left no space for anything else.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: continues without noticing the clock, no wrap-up.
  • Hire: recovers, completes boxes and one deep dive.
  • Strong hire: names the overrun, resets with a stated budget, and still delivers failure modes and cost.

questions.promptHtml: "System design" can mean several different rounds. How do you tell which one you are in and how does your approach change?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Candidates who answer an LLD round with boxes and arrows, or a mobile round with backend-only boxes, lose the round on format.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I ask early, or listen for cues. HLD wants boxes, data flow, storage and scale. LLD or machine coding wants classes, interfaces, patterns and runnable code. API design wants endpoints, pagination, idempotency, versioning. A project deep dive wants "why not X?" at every box. Domain-specific rounds, like Android, want offline sync, image loading, push and large lists.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
HLD      "design Twitter"        boxes, scale, storage, trade-offs
LLD      "design parking lot"    classes, interfaces, patterns, code
API      "design payments API"   endpoints, idempotency, errors, versioning
Project  "walk me through..."    own architecture, defend every choice
Mobile   "Android photo feed"    offline cache, paging, upload retry, battery

Example mobile prompt: 20 posts per page, 30 KB thumbnails, so a page is 600 KB, roughly 0.1 s of transfer at 50 Mbps plus latency. Design: Paging 3 with a Room cache as single source of truth, WorkManager for retried uploads. The backend is the smaller part.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Backend-only boxes in a mobile design.
  • HLD-depth answer in an LLD round (they want classes and code).
  • Not asking which flavour it is.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you recognise a project deep dive? -> The prompt is about something I built; expect "why this database?" on each box.
  2. Which company leans to which flavour? -> Roughly: payments companies lean API and idempotency; delivery and ride companies lean domain prompts; verify per loop, it changes.
  3. How would you prepare differently for each? -> HLD: blocks plus 15 to 20 problems; LLD: coded patterns; project: rehearse trade-offs for my own system.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Mid: treats all of them as "draw the architecture". Senior: names the round type in the first minute and shapes the deliverable accordingly.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: The same mismatch shows up at work when a design doc written for architects is handed to the implementers who needed an API contract.

questions.contextHtml: The interviewer says exactly: "Design Instagram." Nothing else. They lean back and wait. You have 45 minutes.
questions.promptHtml: What do you say in the first three minutes?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Starts drawing "app servers, a database, S3, CDN" immediately. Or asks twenty questions in a row that do not change the design.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which core features: post photo, follow, feed, like/comment (I propose these four and exclude stories, DMs, ads)? Scale: DAU and posts per day (I will assume 100M DAU, 5M posts/day)? Read/write ratio (assume feeds are far heavier)? Freshness: is a feed a few seconds stale acceptable? One region or global?
  2. Immediate mitigation: I write the agreed scope and the assumptions on the board, and say "correct me if any of these is wrong".
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The hard parts are likely feed generation (fan-out), media storage and delivery, and ranking. I propose one for the deep dive and ask which they prefer.
  4. How I'd verify each: A 2-minute estimate: 5M posts/day = about 58 writes/s; feed loads 100M x 10 = 1B/day = about 11,600/s average, about 35,000/s peak; media 5M x 2.3 MB = about 11.5 TB/day.
  5. Root cause: Not applicable; this is scoping. The numbers say read-heavy plus blob-heavy: cache, CDN, object storage.
  6. Fix: Move to the API and high-level design with those numbers visible.
  7. Prevention: Keep questions to those that change the design (scale, consistency, scope).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not start with the database, and not interrogate for 10 minutes.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Just assume anything you want" -> I state my assumptions anyway and write them down; the stated assumptions are the signal.
  • "Include stories and DMs too" -> I treat them as phase 2, cost the extra scope, and ask what to cut to fit 45 minutes.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: two candidates got the same prompt; one asked about read/write ratio and found a 40:1 ratio, the other designed a symmetric write path. The first was rated stronger purely on scoping.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: draws immediately, no assumptions.
  • Hire: 4 to 5 sharp questions, stated scope, rough numbers.
  • Strong hire: scope, assumptions and numbers on the board, and a proposed deep dive chosen from them.

questions.contextHtml: You are at minute 8 of a ride-hailing design, mid-way through estimates, with a clean plan: high-level 10-20, deep dive 20-38. The interviewer interrupts: "Skip the boxes. How does matching a rider to a driver work when 50,000 drivers ping location every 4 seconds?"
questions.promptHtml: How do you respond, and how do you treat your plan?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Let me finish the high-level design first, I will get there." The interviewer is telling you where the signal is; refusing to follow reads as inflexible.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: One quick check: "Matching radius and latency target? I will assume nearest available driver within 2 s."
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pivot at once and say "happy to go straight there; I will sketch the boxes as they become relevant".
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The interviewer cares about write-heavy location ingestion (50,000 / 4 s = 12,500 updates/s) and spatial lookup.
  4. How I'd verify each: Do the arithmetic aloud: 12,500 writes/s is trivial for an in-memory geo index sharded by region cell; the lookup is "drivers in cells near rider".
  5. Root cause: Not applicable; the point is adapting the plan.
  6. Fix: Sketch driver app -> location service -> in-memory geo index (cells), matching service queries nearby cells, offers to top drivers sequentially. Then return to skipped items (API, durable ride state) later.
  7. Prevention: Treat the timeline as a guide, not a script.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not abandon wrap-up; I will still reserve the final 5 minutes.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• After 10 minutes the interviewer says "ok, now back to the overall design" -> I draw it now with the matching component already placed.
  • Driver location needs durability? -> No for the live index (ephemeral, rebuilt from the next ping); yes for trip trace if needed for billing, via a stream.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a candidate with a perfect plan lost points for saying "I have not finished" three times; feedback read "did not take the hint".

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: refuses to pivot.
  • Hire: pivots and answers the matching question with mechanism.
  • Strong hire: pivots, uses a number from the prompt (12,500/s), and later stitches the answer back into the overall design.

questions.promptHtml: What kind of notes does an interviewer write about a candidate during a design round, and how do you produce the positive ones on purpose?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shows whether the candidate understands that unexplained choices earn nothing and that thinking aloud is the scoring surface.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Interviewers write short concrete phrases. Positive: "asked read/write ratio before choosing storage", "used numbers to decide on a cache", "named the queue failure mode unprompted", "took a hint gracefully". Negative: "chose Kafka without saying why", "could not explain cache and DB consistency", "silent". I produce positives by giving every choice a reason, an alternative and a failure mode, out loud.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Choice -> Reason -> Alternative -> Failure mode -> Positive note

Naming a technology is cheap; defending it scores. Every pick is a reversible decision in the interview, but often a one-way door in real life (a primary key scheme or database engine is hard to undo). Saying so is itself a signal: "Postgres first, I can shard later, but changing the primary key scheme later is painful".

Example sentence: "Redis for the feed cache: 100M users x 800 post IDs x 8 bytes = 640 GB is too big for one node, so I cluster it and cache only the active 20%, about 130 GB."

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Buzzword lists (Kafka, Redis, Cassandra) with no why.
  • Silence; the interviewer cannot credit what they cannot hear.
  • Dismissing the interviewer's concern instead of engaging.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not just use X instead? -> State the trade-off honestly; "X is simpler and fine until N; I chose Y because the number says M".
  2. What if the interviewer disagrees with your choice? -> Engage, restate their concern, show the condition under which they are right.
  3. How do you show the one-way-door awareness? -> Say which decisions are costly to reverse (public API, ID scheme, partition key) and which are cheap (cache TTL, CDN vendor).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Mid: names the tools. Senior: reason, alternative, failure mode, and reversibility for each tool.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Design review comments sound the same: "why this queue?" A choice with no stated alternative is the one that gets rewritten six months later.

questions.contextHtml: You are designing a notifications system. Early on you say "I will put Kafka between the API and the senders." The interviewer asks: "Why Kafka?" Your numbers: 10M notifications/day, which is about 115/s average and about 350/s peak. Team size is 4. The senders call email and SMS vendors that rate limit at 100 requests/s.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Kafka is scalable and industry standard." No numbers, no alternative, no failure mode.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is ordering per user required? Is losing a notification acceptable? Does the team already run Kafka?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Admit the volume does not need Kafka's throughput: 350/s is tiny.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: What I actually need is durable buffering, retries, and smoothing the burst to the vendor's 100/s limit. A managed queue (SQS-style or RabbitMQ) provides that with less operations. Kafka is justified only for replay, many consumers, or much higher volume.
  4. How I'd verify each: Check if any consumer needs replay of history (e.g. analytics); count consumers; check team expertise.
  5. Root cause: I reached for a familiar tool before using the numbers.
  6. Fix: Use a managed queue with a dead-letter queue, a rate-limited worker pool at 100/s per vendor, idempotency key per notification so retries do not duplicate. Say that I would move to Kafka if consumers or volume grew 10x to 100x, and that this is a reversible decision if producers hide behind an internal interface.
  7. Prevention: Add queue-depth and age-of-oldest-message alerts.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not add Kafka for a 350/s load with a 4 person team: every box needs on-call and a failure story.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Marketing wants a 5M-user blast in 10 minutes -> that is about 8,300/s, above vendor limits; I would need multiple vendors or a longer window, and a separate low-priority queue so transactional messages are not blocked.
  • The queue is down -> API returns 202 with outbox in the DB (transactional outbox) and a relay retries later.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team ran a 3-broker Kafka for 200 messages/s; the cluster's upgrade work exceeded the feature work for a quarter.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "it is scalable".
  • Hire: uses the numbers and offers a simpler alternative.
  • Strong hire: also states the rate-limit shaping, the failure story, and the trigger for revisiting.

questions.contextHtml: You are interviewing for a senior Android role. Prompt: "Design the Android client of a photo feed with infinite scroll, offline viewing, and photo upload." You begin to draw load balancers and Cassandra. The interviewer says nothing but writes.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Backend-only boxes. Mobile constraints (battery, flaky network, process death, memory) never appear.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Scope of the client: do I design the backend too, or assume a paginated API exists? Offline: read-only cache or also queued posts? Image sizes and counts? Minimum Android version and low-end devices?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reset: "this is a client-focused round, I will assume a cursor-paginated feed API and a pre-signed upload API".
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Hard parts are list scalability, offline consistency, upload reliability, and image memory.
  4. How I'd verify each: Numbers: 20 posts per page, 30 KB thumbnails, so 600 KB per page, about 0.1 s at 50 Mbps plus latency; 10 pages is 6 MB, so cache on disk and size the memory cache by device class.
  5. Root cause: Not applicable.
  6. Fix: Paging 3 with RemoteMediator, Room as the single source of truth, image loader with disk and memory caches, WorkManager for uploads with exponential backoff and an idempotency key, pre-signed URL so a 5 MB image goes direct to object storage. Handle process death by persisting upload state.
  7. Prevention: Metrics: time to first content, upload success rate, crash-free sessions, cache hit rate.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not put the DB as source of truth AND the network as source of truth; pick one (Room) to avoid flicker and conflicts.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• User deletes a post offline -> queue the delete, mark tombstone locally, reconcile on sync; last-writer rules stated.
  • Upload fails at 90% -> resumable chunked upload; verify support on the storage API.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: an otherwise strong backend candidate got a "no hire" for a mobile round because the notes read "never mentioned the client".

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: backend only.
  • Hire: paging, local cache, upload retry.
  • Strong hire: also single source of truth, process death, idempotency, metrics, low-end device budgeting.

questions.contextHtml: You did a mock interview for a senior role and got feedback: "Mid-level. The design was correct, but no hire at senior." Your design for a rate limiter was clean: gateway, Redis counters, sliding window. Your transcript shows: 2 clarifying questions, no numbers, one deep dive on the algorithm, no mention of Redis failing, no cost, and you silently drew for 4 minutes at one point.
questions.promptHtml: Analyse the feedback and describe what you will change.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The interviewer was too harsh; my design was right." Misses that the rubric is multi-axis and that correctness is only one axis.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Ask the mock interviewer which axes were weak, and what a senior answer would have added.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Map each observation to an axis: estimation (no numbers), operations (no failure story, no cost), communication (4 silent minutes), trade-offs (only one algorithm shown).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Gap is not knowledge but signal production: I did the work in my head and did not say it.
  4. How I'd verify each: Re-do the same prompt with a checklist and record it; count how many of the 7 axes got an explicit sentence.
  5. Root cause: Optimised for "correct design" only.
  6. Fix: Add: "1M req/s peak across 10M users, Redis handles about 100K ops/s per node, so I need about 10+ shards by client id"; failure mode: "if Redis is down I fail open for non-critical routes and closed for login, with local in-memory limits as backup"; cost: Redis memory for counters; compare token bucket vs sliding window.
  7. Prevention: Think aloud; say "I am drawing X" while drawing; use a 7-axis checklist during practice.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not add random extra boxes to look senior; depth on one or two parts beats width.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What would a staff-level answer add? -> Multi-region consistency of limits, rollout and migration, org-wide policy ownership.
  • Fail open or closed? -> Depends on the endpoint: abuse risk vs availability; state the decision gravity.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a candidate rewatched a recording and found 90 seconds of silence at the exact moment the interviewer had a key question; adding narration alone raised the next rating.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the interviewer.
  • Hire: maps feedback to axes and plans practice.
  • Strong hire: gives concrete added sentences with numbers, failure handling and cost.

questions.contextHtml: You have a senior system design onsite in 3 weeks. You work full time and can study about 8 hours per week (24 total). You know basic caching and databases. You have watched many walk-through videos but have never drawn a design on a blank page. A friend suggests memorising 40 designs.
questions.promptHtml: Build the plan and justify what you drop.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Watch more videos and memorise the popular designs." Passive and brittle: a new prompt breaks it.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which round types in the loop (HLD, LLD, project deep dive)? Which companies and domains? Which building blocks am I weakest at?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop passive videos; start blank-page practice in week 1.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Biggest risk is lack of active recall and timed delivery, not lack of knowledge.
  4. How I'd verify each: After each problem, compare against a reference and list what I missed; track misses.
  5. Root cause: Pattern recognition comes from assembling blocks repeatedly, not from reading.
  6. Fix: Week 1 (8 h): blocks (load balancer, cache, queue, shard, replica, CDN) and estimation drills. Week 2: storage, caching, messaging deep dives plus 4 timed problems. Week 3: 6 timed problems (45 min plus 15 min review each = 6 h) and 2 mocks with a friend, record one. Ten problems at 1 hour each is 10 hours, which fits.
  7. Prevention: Keep a list of "misses"; re-drill those blocks.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not memorise 40 designs; I memorise reasons and numbers (like 62^7 for 7-char keys). I drop rare topics unless the loop needs them.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Only 1 mock partner available -> self-record and review; the recording exposes silence and rambling.
  • A prompt you never practised appears -> map it to blocks: it is usually read-heavy or write-heavy with a known pattern.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a candidate who had memorised designs froze when the interviewer changed "chat" to "chat with 5M-member channels"; one who had practised blocks adapted the fan-out strategy live.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: videos and memorising.
  • Hire: blocks, timed problems, mocks, review.
  • Strong hire: weakness-driven schedule, review loop, hour math that fits the 24 hours.

questions.contextHtml: Prompt: an internal HR leave-approval tool for a company of 5,000 employees. Peak 10 requests/s. You have drawn: API gateway, 6 microservices, Kafka, Redis cluster, Cassandra, and multi-region active-active. The interviewer asks: "Is that the simplest thing that works?"

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Defends everything: "it is future-proof." Interviewers read this as not using numbers, and as not owning operations cost.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Availability need (office hours? 99.9%?), compliance, expected growth, data size.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Concede: at 10 req/s one modest app server and one Postgres do the job.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: I added components for their own sake, not for a requirement.
  4. How I'd verify each: 5,000 employees x maybe 2 requests/day is 10,000/day, about 0.1/s average; even 100x peak is trivial. Data: 5,000 x 20 leave records/year x 1 KB = 100 MB/year.
  5. Root cause: Pattern-matching to a big-company diagram.
  6. Fix: Load balancer with 2 stateless app instances (for availability, not load), one Postgres primary with a standby and backups, email via an outbox table and a worker. Add components only when a number requires them.
  7. Prevention: Every box must have a stated reason, an owner and a failure story.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not add Kafka, Redis or multi-region; I name the trigger for each (e.g. cache when read QPS is above what one replica serves, multi-region when a regional outage cost exceeds the operating cost).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Company grows to 500,000 employees -> 100x, still about 10 to 100 req/s, so only the data and the audit requirements change.
  • Regulator requires audit history for 7 years -> append-only audit table, partition by year, archive.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team replaced a single Postgres app with 9 services for a 20 req/s product; two quarters later they re-merged it. The interviewer's question is that quarter in one sentence.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: defends the complexity.
  • Hire: simplifies with numbers.
  • Strong hire: simplifies, states the growth triggers for each removed component, and notes the real operational risks (backups, standby, audit).
